title: Two ways (Didache 1)
hookLine: there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and great is the difference
tomorrow: how does a hillside of scattered wheat become one loaf?

lines: ONE OF LIFE, ONE OF DEATH.
cards: A maps app offers two routes: the fast one, and the one without tolls. Most days hold forks like that, so small nobody notices choosing. A short old book opens right at one.
There are two ways, it says, one of life and one of death, and great is the difference between them. No greeting. No author's name.
Just the fork, in the first line. The book is the Didache, a Greek word for teaching. Tradition calls it the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles.

teach.b: So what does the way of life ask? The Didache starts where Jesus starts. First, love the God who made you.

teach.h: WHAT YOU WOULDN'T WANT, DON'T DO.
teach.b: Then a line with a twist: whatever you wouldn't want done to you, don't do to another.
Jesus says it as a do: "all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets." The Didache gives it as a line you won't cross.
The fork itself is older still. Moses sets it before Israel: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." And that golden line has a well-known Jewish cousin.
The Talmud tells of a man who asks the sage Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot. Hillel answers: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor.
That's the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn.
Here's what's shared: the same don't, and the same sense that one plain line can hold a whole way of living.
And the honest difference: for Hillel the line sums up the Torah, and the next step is to go and study it.
The Didache sets it inside the way Jesus taught, with love of God first, and leads on to baptism and a shared meal. One line, two homes.

how: The Didache isn't read in most Sunday services, but Christians study it as an early handbook, and its two ways and golden rule echo teaching that churches give new believers.

practice: Bring to mind one fork waiting for you today: a reply, a bit of money, a word about someone who isn't there. Name which way is life, name what usually pulls you the other way, and settle now what you'll do when that pull shows up.
